778.title: Even Devadatta
778.hook: in the Lotus Sutra he too is promised Buddhahood, a Mahayana view (Lotus Sutra, Devadatta chapter)
778.howItsDone: In some Mahayana communities the Lotus Sutra is chanted and studied, and its Devadatta chapter is read as a teaching that awakening reaches everyone; in Theravada communities Devadatta's story is told from the Pali Vinaya and commentaries as a warning about envy and ambition.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Devadatta's plots: hired men, a rock, an elephant, and a split. Your line was the split. Did you take one small step back across a line? Day seven hundred seventy-eight.

What happens to Devadatta in the end? The Pali commentaries tell it starkly. Late in life, tradition says, he set out to see the Buddha and ask forgiveness, and the earth opened and swallowed him before he arrived. The same commentaries add a quieter line: that far in the future, even he will come to awakening. And in a Mahayana scripture, the Lotus Sutra, there's a chapter that carries his name and goes further still. It doesn't begin with Devadatta's crimes. It begins with a king, long ago, who wanted to learn. Today, even Devadatta.
screen: `THE EARTH OPENS.` → `A DOOR LEFT OPEN.` → `A CHAPTER WITH HIS NAME.`

segments.voice: First, the king. In the chapter, the Buddha tells a story from one of his past lives. He was a king, he says, who wanted the highest teaching so much that he was ready to give up his throne for it. He announced that he would serve anyone who could teach him. Second, the seer. A seer came and said he knew a sutra, the Lotus, and would teach it if the king became his servant. So the king served him. He picked fruit, drew water, gathered firewood, prepared food, even let his own body be the seer's seat, and never wearied of it. Third, the name. Then the Buddha says who the seer was. That seer was Devadatta. And because of Devadatta, his good friend, the Buddha says, he came to complete the qualities of a buddha. Fourth, the promise. The chapter then says that after a vast stretch of time, Devadatta himself will become a buddha, named Heavenly King. This is a Mahayana view, and it's fair to say plainly whose it is. Theravada Buddhists read the Pali Vinaya and commentaries, where Devadatta's deeds bring heavy results, though the commentaries also leave that far door open. In some Mahayana schools, the Lotus chapter is read as saying that no one stands outside the reach of awakening, not even the cousin who rolled the rock. Some teachers also read it about enemies: the one who opposed you may turn out, in a long enough view, to be part of what formed you. Neither tradition says what Devadatta did was small. Both keep the warning. The Lotus chapter sets a promise beside it.
screen: `A KING WHO WANTED THE TEACHING.` · `A SEER WHO TAUGHT HIM.` · `THAT SEER WAS DEVADATTA.` · `HE TOO WILL BE A BUDDHA.` · then, large: `EVEN HIM.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: wish one enemy well. Settle, and let the breath slow on its own. Bring to mind someone who has opposed you. Not the worst person you know. Someone in the middle: a rival, a critic, someone who made one season harder. If you practice loving-kindness, you might use the phrases that practice already uses, wishing them well and safe. If not, simply wish them one good thing: a good night's sleep, a kind word today. Wishing them well doesn't approve of anything they did. The Lotus chapter doesn't excuse Devadatta either. Just wish the one good thing, and stay with the breath. The bell holds the time.
Even Devadatta. In the Lotus Sutra, the cousin who split the sangha is named the Buddha's past teacher and promised buddhahood. Today's word.
Your line: even him. Today, when someone who has crossed you comes to mind, wish them one good thing before you move on. Day seven hundred seventy-eight.

779.title: Faces of the sangha
779.hook: wise, powerful, forgetful, proud, gentle: all were welcome
779.howItsDone: Buddhists go for refuge to the Buddha, the dhamma and the sangha, often reciting the three refuges in Pali at the start of a gathering, and teachers retell the disciples' stories to show that people of every temperament walked the path.

segments.voice: Yesterday, even Devadatta, named in the Lotus Sutra as the Buddha's past teacher and promised buddhahood. Your line was even him. Did you wish one good thing to someone who crossed you? Day seven hundred seventy-nine.

Line them up the way the texts remember them. A man the texts call foremost in wisdom. His friend, foremost in powers. A slow monk who couldn't keep a single verse in his head. A former charioteer too proud to take advice from anyone. A cousin so gentle he served as attendant, bringing water and keeping the door. Different speeds, different tempers, different flaws, all in one robe color. None of them was turned away for being who he was. Today, the faces of the sangha.

First, the word. Sangha means community, an assembly. In the narrow sense it's the order of monks and nuns. In a wider sense, some Buddhists use it for everyone who walks the path together. It's the third of the Three Jewels, beside the Buddha and the dhamma, the things a Buddhist goes to for refuge. Second, the wise and the powerful. Sariputta and Moggallana, the two chief disciples, are the faces people expect. The texts praise one for wisdom and the other for power, and the path has met both. Third, the slow and the proud. In a commentary story, Culapanthaka's own brother told him to leave the order, because he couldn't learn one verse. The Buddha handed him a clean white cloth instead, and as he rubbed it gray, he understood. And Channa, the former charioteer, was so stubborn that the Buddha, before he died, said the monks should give him the higher penalty: no one would speak to him or advise him. The Vinaya says that silence brought him to his senses, and he too awakened. Fourth, the same path at different paces. Ananda, gentle and loyal, was still not awakened when the Buddha died. The sangha was never a gallery of finished people. It was a room where people at very different points sat side by side. And the welcome had a shape. It wasn't approval of every flaw. Channa's pride was met with a hard silence. But the silence was meant to bring him back, not to push him out.
screen: `SANGHA: THE COMMUNITY.` · `WISE AND POWERFUL, SIDE BY SIDE.` · `SLOW AND PROUD, STILL WELCOME.` · `ONE PATH, DIFFERENT PACES.` · then, large: `ALL WERE WELCOME.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: accept one flaw in a friend. Settle, and let the breath find its own pace. Bring one friend to mind. Let one of their flaws come up, the habit that wears on you. Running late. Talking over people. Forgetting things you told them. Don't fix it. Don't excuse it, either. Just set it beside everything else they are, the way the sangha set the slow monk beside the wise one. The flaw is real, and the friend is more than the flaw. Rest there for a few breaths. The bell holds the time.
Sangha. The community, assembly: wise, powerful, forgetful, proud and gentle, all welcomed and practicing side by side. Today's word.
Your line: all were welcome. Today, when that friend's flaw shows up, let it pass once without a comment, and notice what else they bring. Day seven hundred seventy-nine.

780.title: The disciples, closed
780.hook: the ones who walked with him, and who we are like
780.howItsDone: Buddhist teachers retell the great disciples' stories in talks and festivals, and in Theravada countries the chief disciples Sariputta and Moggallana are honored together, with images of them standing on either side of the Buddha.

segments.voice: Yesterday, sangha: wise, powerful, forgetful, proud, gentle. Your line was all were welcome. Did one friend's flaw pass once without a comment? Day seven hundred eighty.

Two friends at a festival who suddenly found the show empty. A cousin who remembered everything he heard. A strict elder in a patched robe. A barber ordained ahead of princes. A boy who had never heard the words there isn't. A queen and her mirror, a mother and her mustard seed, a merchant and a grove covered in gold, a sweeper among thrown-away flowers. For weeks now the path has walked beside the people who walked beside the Buddha. Today this part of the path closes, and it leaves one question with you.
screen: `A FESTIVAL, A BARBER, A BOY.` → `A QUEEN, A MOTHER, A SWEEPER.` → `ONE QUESTION.`

segments.voice: First, the friends. Sariputta and Moggallana, who made a pact that whoever found the deathless first would tell the other, and kept it. Wisdom and power, side by side. Second, the rememberers. Ananda kept the door and kept the words. Upali kept the rules. Kassapa kept the strict practices and called the council so the teaching wouldn't be lost. Anuruddha, the boy who never heard there isn't, learned what the work of the fields costs. Third, the women and the lay followers. Mahapajapati went first. Khema, Patacara, Dhammadinna and Kisa Gotami taught and were taught. Visakha and Anathapindika gave, and Citta, a householder, taught monks. Fourth, the warnings and the welcome. Slow Culapanthaka and the sweeper Sunita were let in. Proud Channa was met with silence and came back. Devadatta split the sangha, and even he has a far door left open in the texts. Notice how the Anguttara Nikaya remembers them. It has a chapter naming the foremost, and each is foremost in something different: one in wisdom, one in power, one in learning, one in the discipline, a nun in teaching, a layman in giving. It's a gallery, not a ladder. And when the Buddha was dying, he named no one to take his place. In the Mahaparinibbana Sutta he tells Ananda that the teaching and the discipline will be their teacher. So the disciples aren't a line of successors. They're a set of mirrors. Somewhere among them is a face that looks a little like yours.
screen: `THE FRIENDS: WISDOM AND POWER.` · `THE ONES WHO REMEMBERED.` · `THE WOMEN AND THE LAY FOLLOWERS.` · `THE WARNINGS AND THE WELCOME.` · then, large: `WHICH ONE ARE YOU?`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: name the disciple you're most like. Settle, and let the breath come in and go out. Let the faces pass by slowly. The friend who ran to share good news. The attendant who held the door. The one who couldn't remember a verse. The proud one. The grieving mother. The generous merchant. The restless prince. One of them will stay a little longer than the others. Don't choose the one you'd like to be. Choose the one you are, this season, flaws included. Then sit with them for a while, as company. The bell holds the time.
The disciples. The people who walked with the Buddha: wise, slow, proud, grieving, generous, and each remembered by name. Today's word.
Your line: which one are you. Today, when you catch yourself acting like your disciple, at their best or their worst, name them quietly. Day seven hundred eighty.

781.title: The sisters' songs
781.hook: the poems of the first nuns, kept in the Pali canon in their own voices
781.howItsDone: The Therigatha is read and studied by Buddhists and scholars as the voices of the early nuns, and its verses are recited in Pali in some Theravada communities and quoted in talks about women's place in the sangha.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the disciples, closed. Your line was which one are you. Did you catch yourself acting like your disciple, and name them? Today a new part of the path opens: songs of the elders. Day seven hundred eighty-one.

A woman remembers her kitchen and says she's free of it. Another watches a lamp go out. Another is told she can finally sleep. Another left her room again and again before she could sit still. Until now the path has told stories about the women of the early sangha. Now they speak. In a small book of the Pali canon, the nuns of the Buddha's time talk about their own lives, their losses and their freedom, in verse. The book has a name, and it's today's word.
screen: `A KITCHEN, A LAMP, A ROBE.` → `NOW THEY SPEAK.` → `IN VERSE.`

segments.voice: First, the name. Therigatha. A theri is an elder nun, a senior woman of the order. A gatha is a verse. So the title is simply the verses of the elder nuns. Second, the verse. These aren't sermons or rules. They're short poems, some only a few lines, some much longer, each put in the mouth of a nun, usually named. Some are her own words about what her life was and how she came free. Some are words spoken to her, by the Buddha or a teacher, that the collection keeps as hers. Third, her own voice. The poems talk about very ordinary things: kitchen tools, husbands, children lost, a body growing old, a restless night, a lamp. Awakening in these poems doesn't happen far away from ordinary life. It happens in the middle of it, and the women say so plainly, sometimes with grief, sometimes with a sharp joke. Fourth, the place they were kept. The Therigatha sits in the Pali canon, in the collection of shorter books, beside a companion book of verses by elder monks, where the path already met Sunita and Sopaka. A later commentary adds a life story for each nun, and scholars debate how old each poem is and how the collection came together. Some readers count it among the earliest collections of women's poetry anywhere. Whatever the dating, the canon did something worth noticing. It kept women of the early sangha speaking about their own awakening, in the first person, and handed their words down.
screen: `THERI: AN ELDER NUN.` · `GATHA: A VERSE.` · `SHORT POEMS IN HER VOICE.` · `KEPT IN THE PALI CANON.` · then, large: `HER OWN WORDS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: read one short poem. Any poem will do: one from a book on your shelf, one a friend sent, one you remember from school. Read it slowly, once. If you can, read it aloud, quietly. Then choose one line, the one that stays. Settle, let the breath find its pace, and sit with that line. Don't explain it to yourself. Just let it repeat, the way, tradition says, the nuns' verses were recited and remembered before anyone wrote them down. The bell holds the time.
Therigatha. The verses of the elder nuns, a book of the Pali canon where the early nuns speak of their own lives and their own freedom. Today's word.
Your line: her own words. Today, carry the one line you chose, and say it to yourself once more before evening. Day seven hundred eighty-one.

782.title: Sleep softly
782.hook: an unnamed nun is told: sleep softly in the robe you made, your passion stilled like herbs dried in a pot (Therigatha 1.1)
782.howItsDone: Readers of the Therigatha meet this short poem first, and teachers in some Buddhist communities use it to speak about rest and contentment as part of the path, not a break from it.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Therigatha, the verses of the elder nuns. Your line was her own words. Which line did you carry from your poem? Today, the first poem in the book. Day seven hundred eighty-two.

A robe, sewn by the woman who will wear it. A pot on a shelf where herbs have dried out. And a voice saying: sleep softly. That's nearly the whole of the first poem in the Therigatha. It's only a few lines long, and the nun it speaks to has no name. The heading calls her a certain elder nun, and that's all. The book of the nuns' own words opens not with a queen or a famous teacher, but with a woman nobody wrote down by name. Today, the opening poem.
screen: `A ROBE SHE SEWED.` → `HERBS DRIED IN A POT.` → `A NUN WITH NO NAME.`

segments.voice: First, the nun with no name. Some readers find a quiet welcome in that: the first words of the collection go to someone whose name wasn't kept. She could be anyone who sat in a robe and practiced. Second, the robe. In the poem she is told to sleep softly, wrapped in the robe she made herself. Her rest isn't borrowed. She's resting inside her own work, a robe she made for herself. Third, the herbs. The reason she can sleep, the voice says, is that her passion is stilled, like herbs dried in a pot. Green leaves are full of sap. Leave them in a pot and the moisture goes out of them. They don't fight. They just dry. The craving that used to pull at her has lost its sap in the same way. There's nothing left in it to sprout. Fourth, what the poem asks of her. Not to strive harder. Not to teach anyone. Not to prove anything. It says sleep. Freedom, in this first poem, is pictured as rest after long work. In Pali the phrase is sukham supahi, sleep at ease, and sukha is the ordinary word for ease and happiness, the word that stands across from dukkha, suffering. So the book of the nuns begins with permission. A woman is told she can lie down, wrapped in what she made, and sleep without anything tugging at her.
screen: `A NUN WITH NO NAME.` · `A ROBE SHE MADE HERSELF.` · `LIKE HERBS DRIED IN A POT.` · `REST AFTER LONG WORK.` · then, large: `SLEEP SOFTLY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: rest in something you made. Settle, and let the breath lengthen on its own. Find one thing nearby that your own hands made or shaped: a meal, a made bed, a folded sweater, a cleaned counter, a page you wrote. If nothing is within reach, choose one from memory. Let your attention rest on it, the way she rested in her robe. Nothing to improve. Nothing to add. Just rest in something finished. The bell holds the time.
Sleep softly. The first poem of the Therigatha: a nun with no name, told to rest in the robe she made, her passion stilled like herbs dried in a pot. Today's word.
Your line: herbs dried in a pot. Tonight, before sleep, lay a hand on one thing you made today, and let the day be finished. Day seven hundred eighty-two.

783.title: Like the full moon
783.hook: Punna is told to fill herself with good things, like the moon on the fifteenth night (Therigatha, Punna)
783.carry: a little more light each evening
783.howItsDone: In Theravada communities the full-moon day is an observance day, uposatha, when lay Buddhists may visit the temple, take extra precepts and listen to teaching, and verses like Punna's are read as pictures of gradual growth on the path.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the nun with no name, told to rest in the robe she made. Your line was herbs dried in a pot. Did you lay a hand on something you made and let the day finish? Day seven hundred eighty-three.

A thin curve of light low in the evening sky. The next night, a little wider. Then wider again. Nothing is bolted onto the moon. Night by night, more of its face catches the light, until one night the whole round face is lit. A short poem in the Therigatha is built on that picture, and it's spoken to a nun named Punna. Yesterday's poem pictured freedom as something drying out. Today's pictures it as something filling up. Today, like the full moon.
screen: `A THIN CURVE OF LIGHT.` → `WIDER, NIGHT BY NIGHT.` → `THE WHOLE FACE LIT.`

segments.voice: First, the name. Some readers hear a play on it: in Pali, Punna sounds like the word for full. On that hearing, a woman called full is told how to become full. Second, the filling. The poem tells her to fill herself with good things, the good qualities of the teaching. Here the picture is of a vessel being filled. Third, the moon. She is to fill herself like the moon on the fifteenth night, the night it comes full. The moon doesn't get there by force. It gets there a night at a time, a little more light each evening. Fourth, the darkness. With wisdom made full, the poem says, she will tear through the great mass of darkness. A full moon lights a whole field at night, so you can see the path in front of you. That's what the poem promises wisdom does. Put the two poems side by side, yesterday's and today's. Herbs drying in a pot. A moon filling night by night. One is about what goes out of a person, the craving losing its sap. The other is about what comes in, good qualities, growing steadily. The Therigatha holds both pictures without choosing between them. Some teachers call letting go and filling up two sides of one path. And the full-moon nights had a place in the early sangha too: they were observance days, uposatha, when the community gathered.
screen: `A NAME THAT SOUNDS LIKE FULL.` · `FILL YOURSELF WITH GOOD THINGS.` · `LIKE THE MOON ON THE FIFTEENTH.` · `WISDOM TEARS THE DARKNESS.` · then, large: `LIKE THE FULL MOON.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: fill the day with one good thing. Settle, and let the breath come and go. Choose one good thing you can add before tonight. Small is fine: a kind message, a short walk outside, a meal made with care, a page of something worth reading. See where it fits: the hour, the place. Not a whole full moon today. Just one night's more light. Then let the choice rest, and stay with the breath. The bell holds the time.
Punna. The nun told to fill herself with good things the way the moon fills, until wisdom breaks through the dark. Today's word.
Your line: a little more light each evening. Today, add the one good thing you chose, and tonight, if the sky is clear, look for the moon, whatever shape it's in. Day seven hundred eighty-three.

784.title: Free of three crooked things
784.hook: Mutta: free from the mortar, the pestle and her crooked husband (Therigatha, Mutta)
784.howItsDone: Mutta's short poem in the Therigatha is read by Buddhists and scholars as a frank voice from the early nuns, where freedom from household burdens opens onto freedom from birth and death.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Punna, told to fill herself with good things like the full moon. Your line was a little more light each evening. What one good thing did you add to the day? Day seven hundred eighty-four.

Thud. Thud. Thud. A heavy pestle coming down into a mortar, pounding grain, the sound of a household kitchen in the Buddha's India. In the Therigatha, a nun named Mutta remembers that sound. She also remembers a man. And in a poem only a few lines long, she counts them up: three crooked things, and she's free of every one. Some of the nuns' poems are solemn. This one opens almost with a shout. Today, Mutta's poem.
screen: `THUD, THUD, THUD.` → `A MORTAR AND A PESTLE.` → `AND A MAN.`

segments.voice: First, the three. Mutta says she is freed, well freed, from three crooked things: the mortar, the pestle, and her crooked husband. The mortar and pestle were the daily work of pounding grain. The husband, the poem says plainly, was crooked. Why the tools are called crooked too, the poem doesn't say. Some readers think of their bent shapes, some of the bent back of the woman working them all day. Second, the same word. The poem puts the man and the kitchen tools under one word. It's sharp, and it's funny, and the Pali canon kept it. Third, the turn. Then the poem steps from the small freedom to the large one. She is freed from birth and death, it says, and what led her back into becoming has been pulled out by the root. The kitchen was a real weight. In the tradition, birth and death are the weight under every other weight. The poem names both, one after the other, in her own voice. Fourth, a kitchen as a doorway. Mutta doesn't begin with lofty words about release. She begins with the things that bent her back. The freedom the whole path aims at starts, in this poem, from something anyone could point to: a mortar, a pestle, a hard marriage. The poem isn't a verdict on kitchens or on marriage. It's one woman telling plainly what held her, and what doesn't anymore.
screen: `MORTAR, PESTLE, HUSBAND.` · `THREE THINGS, ONE WORD: CROOKED.` · `FREE FROM BIRTH AND DEATH.` · `A KITCHEN AS A DOORWAY.` · then, large: `SO FREED.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: name one freedom you have. Settle, and let the breath move on its own. Look at your life as it is today. Find one thing you are free of, or free to do, that hasn't always been true. A job you left. A habit that loosened. A fear that shrank. A door you can open now. Name it plainly, the way Mutta named her mortar. You don't have to feel grateful on command. Just say what it is, and let it sit beside the breath. The bell holds the time.
Mutta. The nun whose poem says she is freed from mortar, pestle and crooked husband, and then from birth and death. Today's word.
Your line: so freed. Today, when you pick up a tool you don't love, a mop, a keyboard, a steering wheel, name the one freedom you found. Day seven hundred eighty-four.
